Entries are officially open for The Hindu Best Places to Work 2027 Awards, powered by WorkL . Leadership teams across India are encouraged to act decisively and enter today.
The entry process is fast and simple. Registering your organisation takes just 10 minutes, and the brief, anonymous survey requires less than 5 minutes for your employees to complete.
Register your organisation today and complete your employee survey before the entry window closes on February 26, 2027 to become recognised as a Best Place to Work in India: Enter The 2027 Awards.
For years, India’s corporate landscape has been held up as a global benchmark for workplace engagement and high employee ambition. Yet beneath the headlines of economic growth and rapid technological expansion, a subtle shift is taking place within our offices and remote teams. WorkL’s latest 2026 data for India reveals that employee engagement has contracted to 78%, down three percentage points year on year. Concurrently, job satisfaction has slipped to 80%, while employee flight risk has concerningly climbed three percentage points to 14%.
These figures are not merely statistical dips; they signal a growing fatigue among Indian professionals. Having long set the standard for passion and resilience, India’s workforce is now sending a clear message: career ambition cannot come at the cost of personal wellbeing.
To understand what is driving this sentiment, one must look at how the nature of work itself is changing. India has emerged as the global leader in artificial intelligence integration, with ADP Research’s People at Work 2026 Report finding that 80% of Indian employees use AI multiple times a week, and 41% use it daily. Furthermore, Microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index highlights that 32% of Indian professionals are now “frontier users” deploying AI agents in complex, multi-step workflows.
However, rapid automation has birthed a subtle productivity paradox. As AI speeds up routine execution, manager expectations have escalated without a matching evolution in how human effort is valued. WorkL’s latest 2026 data reflects this gap: reward and recognition took the sharpest hit in India, dropping four percentage points to 75% in 2026, alongside a matching four percentage point decline in information sharing (78%). When employees feel their human judgment is reduced to tracking metrics and that corporate decisions are made behind closed doors, motivation quickly wanes.
This gap is compounded by a loss of individual agency. Empowerment dropped to 78% in 2026, reflecting a widespread contraction in decision-making autonomy and manager relationships. In qualitative feedback across Indian organisations, employees point to long shifts, weekend intrusion, and aggressive deadlines as constant pain points. The modern Indian workplace has increasingly blurred the lines between professional duties and private life. Workers are now calling for firm digital boundaries, such as strict policies against work calls or messages after 8 pm, alongside friction-free leave approval processes.
The drop in wellbeing in India (down three percentage points to 77% in 2026) and job satisfaction also stems from a structural shift in employee expectations. The rapid growth of Global Capability Centres across India, detailed in the JLL India GCC Guide 2026, has raised the cultural and operational bar. Hosting over 2,000 GCCs employing nearly 2.4 million professionals, India’s talent pool now directly compares local employer experiences with mature, global standards.
In India, an employer is rarely seen as just a place to earn a monthly salary; it is viewed as a launching pad for long-term career growth. When routine entry-level execution is automated, mid-career professionals face immense pressure to adapt. Across sectors, employees have voiced a strong desire for structured upskilling, clear promotion pathways, sponsored technical certifications, and fast-track technical progression. If an organisation fails to provide these growth engines, ambitious professionals will naturally seek them elsewhere.
At the same time, workplace friction extends to the physical environment. Lower scores in operational support coincide with urgent calls for fundamental workplace dignity: reliable laptops, high-speed internet, ergonomic seating, clean washrooms, wholesome canteen food, and safe corporate cab services for late-running shifts. Sustainable high performance is impossible when fundamental daily needs are neglected.
Reversing these trends requires a shift from reactive management to continuous listening. Leaders can no longer rely on yearly reviews to gauge morale; they need real-time, data-driven insight into how their workforce actually feels.
This is precisely where The Hindu Best Places to Work 2027 Awards, powered by WorkL, offer a clear route forward. Built on a proven 27-question engagement framework developed by behavioural scientists and psychologists, the initiative provides leadership teams with actionable insights. Through dynamic dashboards, AI thematic analysis, heatmaps, and flight-risk monitoring, organisations can pinpoint structural friction early and build workplace cultures where people genuinely thrive.
Entering the awards allows companies to benchmark their employee experience against national and global standards, while earning prestigious editorial recognition in The Hindu across print and digital platforms. Winning organisations receive national acclaim and a trusted badge of honour that attracts top-tier talent and reinforces internal pride.
Whether you lead a small business of ten people or an enterprise employing thousands, listening to your workforce is the single most effective business decision you can make this year.
